Fig. 6. Applications of our pipeline in the wild. SDR inputs are shown in the top-left; the main panels show HDR results (using Reinhard [2002] tonemapping) produced by our method; we include intensity scan lines (along the red-dashed line) to further compare HDR and SDR. (a) Fully generative HDR video and in-the-wild examples. A text-to-SDR-video model [Wan et al. 2025] is prompted with “no exterior lighting” to produce a dark SDR input, which our model lifts to HDR (top left). We also show three additional in-the-wild examples. (b) Iconic Moments in HDR. Our pipeline re-grades iconic feature-film frames: Spider-Man clinging to a sun-clipped Manhattan skyline (Spider-Man, 2002); two bright lights shining on Dre Parker in the finale of the Open Kung Fu Tournament (The Karate Kid, 2010); a creature silhouetted against a blown-out SDR sun (Jumanji: The Next Level); and the Ghostbusters encounter with an apparition of Gertrude Aldridge in her mansion (Ghostbusters, 2016). Our method recovers dynamic range in both highlights and shadows while minimizing artifacts from noise or compression. Please see supplementary webpage for videos. Fig. 2. Qualitative comparison between our method (left) and LumiVid [Korem et al. 2026] (right) across five challenging conditions. (a) High-frequency motion: our method preserves spatial structure in a waterfall scene; LumiVid exhibits irregular moiré-like distortions. (b) Scene fidelity: our method reconstructs scene content faithfully; LumiVid produces output that diverges significantly from the input. (c) Temporal consistency: our method maintains stable color across frames; the chapel interior color shifts noticeably in LumiVid’s output. (d) Low-light performance: our method recovers shadow detail; LumiVid introduces prominent pink chrominance artifacts in the same dark regions. (e) Scene-linear output: our explicit linearization stage correctly inverts the CRF; LumiVid’s output retains residual tone-mapping in this scene, indicating an incomplete CRF inversion. See supplementary webpage for videos.

Fig. 4. Overview of our HDR video generation pipeline. Our method consists of two stages. (Left) TheMulti-Exposure Video Model (MEVM) utilizes a flow-matching video transformer (Wan2.2) to generate a linearized multi-exposure video from a single SDR input video𝑉𝐶𝑅𝐹 . The input video is encoded into a latent ?̃?𝐶𝑅𝐹 and temporally concatenated with noise-initialized latent frames for the base (?̃?0), under- (?̃?− ), and over-exposed (?̃?+) outputs. To enable the model to reason across exposures, we introduce an exposure-aware RoPE that augments the pre-trained rotary positional embedding with a learned offset encoding the exposure index 𝑒 , CRF indicator 𝑐 , and relative frame index 𝑟 . After denoising, the VAE decoder is applied independently to each exposure to recover the output multi-exposure videos. (Right) The Video Merging Model (VMM) operates per-frame on the generated exposure bracket. For each frame 𝑖 , per-exposure feature maps 𝐹 𝑖 𝑘 consisting of the SDR image, estimated radiance, and exposure value are fed into an MLP with self-attention across exposures to predict blending weights𝑊 𝑖 𝑘 of the per-exposure radiance estimates 𝑅𝑖 𝑘 , resulting in the final HDR frame 𝐻𝑖 .

Qualitative SDR-to-HDR comparison against single-image baselines HDRCNN [Eilertsen et al. 2017] and LEDiff [Wang et al. 2025b] and the videodomain baseline LumiVid [Korem et al. 2026], alongside our method. HDR outputs are visualized with Reinhard [2002] tonemapping. (a) Two frames from the Stuttgart [2014] and UBC [2014] HDR video benchmarks, illustrating an over-exposed scenario (top) and an under-exposed scenario (bottom). (b) Two frames generated from text-to-SDR-video prompts and then lifted to HDR by each method: “A hallway in an old hotel with most lights off” (top, severely under-exposed) and “A row of sailboats rocking in a harbor on a sunny day” (bottom, over-exposed).
